objectives: In a real conversation, reflect back what the other person said and ask an open question, until they agree you understood them

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Active listening: making people feel heard
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Listen to someone and reflect back what they said so they feel understood.
This lesson builds toward: In a real conversation, you will reflect back what the other person said and ask an open question, until they agree you understood them.
Most arguments get worse because each person is busy planning what to say next. Active listening means you put that aside and really try to understand the other person first.
There are four parts. Give full attention: put the phone down and look at the person. Let them finish without cutting in. Reflect back: say in your own words what you heard, such as "So you felt left out when the schedule changed without warning." Then ask an open question, one that cannot be answered with yes or no, such as "What would have helped?"
Reflecting back is not agreeing. You are only showing that you understood. When people feel heard, they usually calm down and start listening to you too.
Step by step:
- Put your phone away and face the person.
- Let them finish. Do not interrupt or fix it yet.
- Reflect back: "So what I am hearing is..."
- Ask an open question: "What would help?" or "Tell me more about..."
- Check: "Did I get that right?"
Words to know:
- Active listening: listening to understand, then showing the person you understood.
- Reflect back: repeating the main point in your own words.
- Open question: a question that needs more than a yes or no answer.
Try it now: In your next real conversation today, with a teammate, coworker, friend or family member, reflect back one thing they said and ask one open question. Notice how they respond.
You can now listen with full attention, reflect back what you heard and ask an open question.

options: A question that can be answered yes or no
A question that invites the person to explain in their own words
A question you ask in a public place
A question you already know the answer to
check.why: Open questions start with words like what or how and invite a full answer.

check.q: A teammate says, "Coach never plays me in the second half." What would you say?
options: "That's not true."
"You should train harder."
"So you feel you aren't getting a fair chance late in games?"
"I don't want to talk about it."
check.why: Reflecting back shows you heard them before you respond.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Saying what you need with "I" statements
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a blaming sentence into a clear "I" statement.
This lesson builds toward: Given a blaming sentence, you will rewrite it as an "I" statement with a clear request, using the pattern I feel, when, because, could we.
"You always..." and "You never..." make people defend themselves, and then nobody listens. An "I" statement talks about what happened and how it affected you, without attacking the other person.
A simple pattern: "I feel [feeling] when [what happened] because [why it matters]. Could we [request]?" For example, instead of "You never pass me the ball," try "I feel frustrated when I am open and the ball does not come to me, because I want to help us score. Could we look at the film together?"
Keep it to one issue, describe what happened as a camera would see it, and end with a request the person can actually do. Your tone and face matter as much as the words, so keep your voice calm.
Step by step:
- Name one thing that happened, as a camera would see it.
- Name your feeling: frustrated, worried, hurt, stressed.
- Say why it matters to you.
- Ask for one clear, doable change.
Words to know:
- "I" statement: a sentence that starts with your feeling and need, not the other person's fault.
- Request: asking for one specific thing the other person can do.
Try it now: Write down three blaming sentences you have said or heard, for example at work or at home. Rewrite each one as an "I" statement with a clear request. Say the best one out loud.
You can now turn a blaming sentence into an "I" statement with a feeling, a reason and a clear request.

check.q: What is the main difference between an "I" statement and a "you" statement?
options: An "I" statement is always longer
An "I" statement describes your feeling and need instead of blaming
A "you" statement is more polite
There is no difference
check.why: "I" statements share your feeling and need, so the other person does not feel attacked.

check.q: Your roommate leaves dishes in the sink. Which would you say?
options: "I feel frustrated when dishes stay overnight, because I cook early. Could we wash them before bed?"
"You are so lazy."
"You always leave a mess."
"Whatever, I'll do it all myself."
check.why: This follows the I feel, when, because, could we pattern with a clear request.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Starting a hard conversation
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan and open a hard conversation at the right time and place.
This lesson builds toward: For a conversation you have been putting off, you will plan the goal, time, place and opening line of a hard conversation, with an opening line you can say calmly out loud.
Many people avoid hard conversations until they explode. A little planning makes them much easier. First, get clear on what you want: not to win, but to fix the problem and keep the relationship working.
Pick a good time and place: private, not rushed, and not when either of you is angry, tired or hungry. Ask first: "Do you have ten minutes today? I would like to talk about the delivery schedule." A text or email can set up the talk, but have the talk itself in person or on a call when you can, because tone gets lost in writing.
Open with a short, calm first line that names the topic and your goal: "I want us to work well together, and something has been bothering me. Can I share it and then hear your side?" Then use your "I" statement, and switch to listening.
Step by step:
- Write down your goal: what would a good result look like?
- Pick a private time when you are both calm.
- Ask if now is a good time.
- Open with the topic and your goal in one or two sentences.
- Use your "I" statement, then listen.
Words to know:
- Hard conversation: a talk about something difficult, where feelings may run high.
- Opening line: the first sentence or two that start the talk calmly.
Try it now: Think of a conversation you have been putting off. Write your goal in one sentence, choose a time and place, and write your opening line. Read the opening line out loud until it sounds calm and natural.
You can now plan a hard conversation, pick a good moment and open it calmly.

check.q: What should you decide before starting a hard conversation?
options: Who will win
Your goal, a good time and place, and your opening line
What to post online about it
How loud to speak
check.why: Planning the goal, time, place and opening helps the talk start calmly.

check.q: You need to talk to your manager about your hours, but they are rushing to a meeting. What would you do?
options: Bring it up right now in the hallway
Send an angry email
Quit without saying anything
Ask for ten minutes at a calmer time today
check.why: A private, calm time gives the talk a better chance.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Calming conflict and agreeing a way forward

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Calming a heated moment
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Cool down a heated moment, in yourself and in the other person.
This lesson builds toward: When a talk gets heated, you will calm yourself and the other person with slow breathing, calming words or a timed break, without raising your voice or saying "calm down".
When we get angry, the body gets ready to fight: the heart races and it is hard to think clearly. Nothing good gets decided in that state, so the first job is to calm down.
Start with yourself: breathe slowly in for four counts and out for six, unclench your hands and lower your voice. Speak slower and softer than the other person. Name what you see without judging: "I can see this matters a lot to you." Avoid "Calm down!", which usually does the opposite.
If it is still too hot, take a break and set a time to come back: "I want to sort this out. Let's take twenty minutes and talk at 3." If you ever feel unsafe, leave and get help. Your safety comes before any conversation.
Step by step:
- Notice your own signs: fast heart, hot face, tight fists.
- Breathe: in for 4, out for 6, a few times.
- Lower and slow your voice.
- Name the feeling you see: "I can see you are upset."
- If needed, take a break and set a time to come back.
- If you feel unsafe, leave and get help.
Words to know:
- De-escalate: to calm a situation down so it does not get worse.
- Time-out: a short agreed break to cool down, with a time to come back.
Try it now: Practise the 4-in, 6-out breath five times now. Then write two calming sentences you could use: one that names the other person's feeling, and one that asks for a break with a time to come back.
You can now calm yourself, help calm someone else and take a safe break when a moment gets too heated.

options: Breathing in for 4 counts and out for 6 to calm down
Four deep breaths, then six fast ones
Holding your breath for 10 seconds
Breathing only through your mouth
check.why: A longer out-breath helps your body calm down.

check.q: An argument with a customer is getting louder and you are getting angry. What would you do?
options: Raise your voice to be heard
Tell them to calm down
Slow your breathing, lower your voice and name their feeling
Walk away without a word
check.why: Calming yourself first and naming their feeling cools the moment.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Finding what each person really needs
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find the needs behind each side's position and list options that meet both.
This lesson builds toward: Given a disagreement, you will list each side's position and interest and three options that could meet both, before judging any option.
In a conflict, people usually state a position: what they say they want. Behind it is an interest: the reason they want it. Two players both want the same jersey number (position). One wants it for luck; the other wants it because it was a late grandparent's number (interests). Knowing the interest opens up new answers.
Ask "why" questions gently: "What is most important to you about this?" or "What worries you about that plan?" Then share your own interest the same way.
Now list options together, without judging them yet. Aim for at least three. A shop owner and an employee who both want Saturdays off might find: alternate weekends, split shifts, or a paid weekend bonus to bring in extra help. The best option usually meets the most important need on each side.
Step by step:
- Write down each side's position.
- Ask what matters most behind it, and write the interests.
- List at least three options together, without judging yet.
- Pick the option that meets the most important needs on both sides.
Words to know:
- Position: what someone says they want.
- Interest: the real need or reason behind the position.
- Brainstorm: listing many ideas quickly before judging any of them.
Try it now: Take the disagreement you planned in Lesson 3. Write down your position and interest, and your best guess at the other person's. Then list three options that could meet both interests.
You can now find the real needs behind a disagreement and list options that could work for both sides.

check.q: What is an interest in a disagreement?
options: The person's first demand
The need or reason behind what a person asks for
How interesting the argument is
Money owed on a loan
check.why: An interest is the need under a position.

check.q: You and a coworker both want Friday off. What would you do first?
options: Flip a coin right away
Let the louder person win
Go to the boss without talking
Ask why each of you needs Friday and list a few options together
check.why: Finding each person's need opens options that can work for both.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Working out a fair agreement
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a good conversation into a clear written agreement and follow up.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of a conversation, you will write an agreement that says who does what by when and how you will check in, with every part written down and shared.
Many good talks fail because nobody says exactly what happens next. A clear agreement answers three questions: who does what, by when, and how you will check it is working.
Fair means both people can live with it and it treats each side's main need with respect. Say it back out loud: "So, I will cover Tuesday closes, you will cover Saturday mornings, starting next week, and we will check in on the 15th." Then write it down in a text, an email or a shared note so nobody remembers it differently later.
Follow up on the date you set. If it is not working, go back to listening and options; that is normal, not failure. For serious problems, such as harassment, safety, money or legal issues, bring in a manager, HR, a coach, a mediator or another trusted person. You do not have to solve everything alone.
Step by step:
- Say the agreement out loud: who, what, by when.
- Ask: "Can we both live with this?"
- Write it down and send a copy to the other person.
- Set a check-in date.
- Follow up. If it is not working, talk again.
Words to know:
- Agreement: what both people decide to do, said clearly.
- Follow up: checking back later to see if the agreement is working.
- Mediator: a neutral person who helps two sides talk and agree.
Try it now: Final task: hold (or role-play with a friend) the conversation you planned. Reflect back, use one "I" statement, ask what they need, agree on who does what by when, and send a short written summary.
You can now close a hard conversation with a fair, written agreement and follow up on it.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Plan for the talk No clear goal, time or opening line. A one-sentence goal, a calm time and place, and an opening line practiced out loud. Also planned how to take a break if things heat up. Listening Interrupted or jumped to answers without reflecting back. Reflected back at least once and asked an open question. The other person said they felt understood. "I" statement Used blaming "you" sentences. Used at least one clear "I" statement with a request. Stayed with "I" statements even when the talk got hard. Needs and options Only argued positions. Asked what the other person needs and looked at more than one option. Found an option that met important needs on both sides. Written agreement No agreement, or it is vague. A written summary of who does what by when, shared with the other person. Includes a check-in date. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why set a check-in date in an agreement?
options: To see if the agreement is working and fix it if not
To punish whoever breaks it
To end the relationship
Because it is required by law
check.why: A check-in lets both people see if the plan works and adjust it.

check.q: You and your business partner agreed on a plan out loud. What would you do next?
options: Trust you will both remember it the same way
Tell other people your version
Send a short written summary of who does what by when
Wait for problems to show up
check.why: A written summary means nobody remembers it differently.
